questions.stem: A hospital achieves Magnet designation from the American Nurses Credentialing Center. What does this designation primarily recognize?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The organization meets a financial performance threshold based mainly on revenue, operating margin, facility growth, and similar business indicators.","B":"The organization meets a size threshold based mainly on licensed beds, service volume, staffing numbers, and the number of specialty departments overall.","C":"The organization demonstrates nursing excellence, strong professional practice, and quality patient outcomes supported by effective nursing leadership.","D":"The organization demonstrates excellence limited to one technical specialty rather than nursing practice, leadership, and patient outcomes across the health care system."}}
questions.rationale: Magnet recognition is an ANCC designation for nursing excellence and quality patient outcomes supported by strong professional nursing practice and leadership. Option C is correct. Option A incorrectly substitutes financial performance for nursing excellence. Option B incorrectly makes organizational size the defining criterion. Option D incorrectly limits the designation to a single technical specialty.
questions.source_name: American Nurses Credentialing Center — Magnet Recognition Program
questions.source_detail: Current ANCC Magnet guidance describes Magnet as the most prestigious recognition for nursing excellence and quality patient outcomes, with nursing leadership and professional practice central to the model.

questions.stem: A hospital adopts a shared governance model for nursing practice. Which description best reflects this model?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Staff nurses participate through councils or committees with meaningful authority over designated practice, quality, and professional decisions.","B":"Only physicians participate in governance councils because nursing staff do not have a formal role in practice or quality decisions.","C":"Senior administrators make nursing-practice decisions independently while staff nurses provide information but have no designated decision authority.","D":"Formal nursing leadership is eliminated so each staff nurse independently determines practice standards without organizational coordination."}}
questions.rationale: Shared governance gives nurses structured participation and designated decision authority over areas of professional practice and quality. Option A is correct. Option B wrongly excludes nurses. Option C describes a top-down model rather than shared governance. Option D incorrectly equates shared governance with eliminating formal leadership or organizational standards.
questions.source_name: American Nurses Association — Shared Governance in Nursing
questions.source_detail: Current ANA guidance describes shared governance structures in which staff nurse representatives participate in councils or committees and receive authority for designated practice functions.

questions.stem: A nurse manager uses Lewin's Change Theory to plan a practice change. Which action belongs to the first stage of the model?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Evaluate the completed change and compare final outcomes with targets before any effort has been made to prepare staff for a new practice.","B":"Implement the new practice across the unit while staff are actively learning the changed workflow and adapting their daily behavior.","C":"Unfreeze the current state by creating awareness of the need for change and addressing forces or resistance that maintain the status quo.","D":"Refreeze the new practice by stabilizing the changed process and integrating it into routine expectations after implementation."}}
questions.rationale: Lewin's model begins with unfreezing, followed by change/movement and then refreezing. Option C is correct because it describes preparing the system to move away from the status quo and reducing resistance. Option B describes the change/movement stage. Option D describes refreezing. Option A incorrectly places evaluation before preparation and implementation.
questions.source_name: NCBI Bookshelf — Nursing Management and Professional Concepts
questions.source_detail: Open RN content describes Lewin's Unfreeze–Change–Refreeze model and identifies unfreezing as recognizing the need for change and overcoming resistance to the status quo.

questions.stem: A unit uses the PDSA cycle to test a small practice change before wider implementation. What does PDSA stand for?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Practice, Document, Standardize, Audit, a sequence focused mainly on formal documentation after a change is already established in routine care.","B":"Prepare, Deliver, Supervise, Approve, a sequence focused mainly on managerial authorization rather than iterative testing of a practice change.","C":"Plan, Do, Study, Act, an iterative sequence used to test a change, examine what happened, and decide how to adapt the next improvement cycle.","D":"Plan, Delay, Start, Assess, a sequence that postpones action rather than using repeated tests to learn whether a practice change works."}}
questions.rationale: The Institute for Healthcare Improvement defines PDSA as Plan-Do-Study-Act. Option C is correct because the cycle tests a change, studies results, and uses the learning to guide the next action. Options A, B, and D are not the accepted expansion of PDSA and misrepresent the iterative improvement method.
questions.source_name: Institute for Healthcare Improvement — Model for Improvement
questions.source_detail: Current IHI guidance defines PDSA as Plan-Do-Study-Act and describes it as the iterative method used to test and adapt changes.

questions.stem: A hospital compares its infection-rate performance with national or peer-organization data to identify opportunities for improvement. What is this process called?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Benchmarking, because the organization compares performance measures with external standards or peers to identify opportunities for improvement in care.","B":"Random surveillance, because comparison with peer organizations is intended to collect data without using an external performance reference.","C":"Credentialing, because comparing infection rates with external organizations primarily verifies professional qualifications and privileges.","D":"Utilization review, because comparison with national infection rates primarily determines whether an individual service was medically necessary for a client."}}
questions.rationale: Benchmarking compares performance metrics or practices with external standards or peer organizations to understand relative performance and identify opportunities for improvement. Option A is correct. Option B incorrectly removes the comparative purpose. Option C concerns professional qualifications and privileges. Option D addresses service utilization rather than peer performance comparison.
questions.source_name: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality — Benchmarking
questions.source_detail: AHRQ describes benchmarking as evaluating metrics or best practices from other organizations and using comparisons to improve performance.
